problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $4$ along the path $y={x}^{4}$
- The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $x=0$
- The limit does not exist
worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{2({0}^{2})\sqrt{0}}{{0}^{4}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0+0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{4}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}}}{{x}^{4}+({x}^{4})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}+{x}^{8}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}(1+{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2\cancel{{x}^{4}}}{\cancel{{x}^{4}}(1+{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{1+{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+{0}^{4}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,x=0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{2({0}^{2})\sqrt{y}}{{0}^{4}+{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$
